patterns.name: Side Volley
patterns.notes: Alternating side volleys. Each is a wall of projectiles with two openings, so the player must read the gap and move to it rather than stand still.

patterns.name: Diagonal Whip
patterns.notes: A thin chain whips corner to corner: the line is the danger, so the dodge is standing off it, not leaving a band. Two diagonals per bar so the second is read from the first.

patterns.name: Safe Ground
patterns.notes: The floor arms and one patch stays safe. The telegraph draws the refuge positively, so the read is "get to the green square", not "leave the red one" -- the two halves of the same lesson AP01 teaches.

patterns.name: Chain Corridor
patterns.notes: Two parallel chains wall off a safe channel that slides across the arena between bars. The channel is floored by the fairness minimum, so it is always wide enough to stand in -- the play is reaching it in time.

patterns.name: Serpent Chain
patterns.notes: A snake of chain with a slowly drifting midline, then a zig-zag that cuts across it. The sine drift is small enough to follow at a walk.

patterns.name: Spiral Out
patterns.notes: A spiral of projectiles unwinds from the centre. The arm rotates as it fires, so the player is walking against a curve rather than sidestepping a line.

patterns.name: Rhythm Window
patterns.notes: The sweep window stops being static: its centre steps once per beat along gapPath, so the wall has a choreography and the player reads the next position on the pulse.

patterns.name: Spray And Pendulum
patterns.notes: A rotating spray walks its bursts around the arena while a pendulum arm swings back across the path. Both threats advertise their direction before they move.

patterns.name: Spray Rotation
patterns.notes: One spray, one direction, one step per beat: the first two bursts are the lesson and the rest are the test. Swap CW for CCW on the repeat so the read is not memorised.

patterns.name: Alternating Spray
patterns.notes: ALTERNATE spray: the stream walks out and then back, so the gap the player used is the gap that closes next. Two arms with a pendulum fan underneath.

patterns.name: Ring Collapse
patterns.notes: The ring collapses onto the player and then blows back out. The window rotates between the two, so the safe spot is a place, not a memorised angle.

patterns.name: Spray Double Time
patterns.notes: Eighth-note emissions: three blades per bar. The rotation is still one direction, so the read is the same -- only the tempo of the read changes.

patterns.name: Safe Tile Sweep
patterns.notes: Safe tiles carve the floor into islands while a straight wall sweeps across. The wall has one static window, so the tile the player commits to has to be on the window line.

patterns.name: Fan And Spray
patterns.notes: Three fan arms sweeping one way and a spray walking the other. The two rotations are deliberately out of phase: there is a safe wedge, but it moves.

patterns.name: Pendulum Fan
patterns.notes: The fan reverses on a fixed cycle, so its arc is a metronome the player can stand still beside -- as long as they stand on the right side of the turning point.

patterns.name: Spiral Inward
patterns.notes: The same spiral, fired inward and turning the other way. The window is a moving notch on the rim, so the player tracks the rotation rather than a fixed angle.

patterns.name: Shrinking Window
patterns.notes: The sweep window tightens as the wall crosses, so a late entry is a narrower entry. The floor is the fairness minimum: it never closes past what the player fits through.

patterns.name: Laser And Ring Climax
patterns.notes: A rotating spray walks the arena while two lasers close across it, and the bar ends with the ring collapsing onto whatever the player committed to. Every threat advertises itself; the difficulty is that they advertise at once.

patterns.name: Sector Chase
patterns.notes: Wedges of the arena go off in turn, first clockwise in sixths and then anticlockwise in quarters. There is no gap to find -- the whole answer is walking the rim at the sweep's pace, and the reversal is the part that punishes memorising one direction.

patterns.name: Sector And Spray
patterns.notes: The sweep skips every other wedge, so the player is moving twice as far per step, and a rotating spray lays fire across the arena while they do it. The closing ring is the only thing here that asks for a *place* rather than a pace.

patterns.name: Shifting Ground
patterns.notes: The refuge drifts instead of sitting still, and it relocates on the bar: around the circle for two bars -- starting opposite each time, so the drift cannot be camped -- then side to side for two. Standing in the right place is not enough any more; the player has to keep arriving.

patterns.name: Quadrant Rotation
patterns.notes: Only a quarter of the arena is ever safe, and which quarter rotates on the bar. Coarse and rhythmic: the crossing is made on the pulse, not steered, which is the point -- it is the one safe-zone form that is a movement *timing* problem rather than a positioning one.

patterns.name: Chain Formation
patterns.notes: The same squad of chains, re-formed every bar: abreast, fanned out, sweeping on a pivot, then arced. The ask never changes -- find the lane that is not a chain -- so each bar is a fresh read of one familiar verb rather than a new threat.

patterns.name: Floor Stripes
patterns.notes: Where is safe, drawn in bigger and bigger strokes: one row, one column, both at once, then a quarter wedge. The warning length is the escape walk, so the cross telegraphs longer than the strip -- the shapes teach themselves.

patterns.name: Double Jump
patterns.notes: Two jumps back to back, rest, one more. The first taste of a chain.

patterns.name: Triple Chain
patterns.notes: A jump on every beat for a full bar.

patterns.name: Short Gap Chain
patterns.notes: Gap, spike, gap, slide. Mixes the three obstacle answers in one phrase.

patterns.name: Bounce Chain
patterns.notes: Pad launches into a spike clear; the bar ends on a quick double.

patterns.name: Half Beat Jumps
patterns.notes: Syncopated eighths. The jump becomes a way of playing the percussion line.

patterns.name: Rapid Stair
patterns.notes: Rising spikes then a slide, so the phrase resolves downward.

patterns.name: Gravity Entry
patterns.notes: Flip on the downbeat, then keep running on the ceiling without a pause.

patterns.name: Gravity Alternation
patterns.notes: Flip, three jumps along the ceiling, flip again, and land back on the floor for the closing pair. Obstacles are tagged to the surface the player is actually on.

patterns.name: Runner Climax
patterns.notes: Everything at once at eighth-note density. The pattern the whole mode builds toward.

patterns.name: Ceiling Chain
patterns.notes: The full inversion sentence: flip up, jump-slide-jump-jump along the ceiling, gravity restores itself and the phrase resolves with two floor jumps.

patterns.name: Mixed Chain
patterns.notes: Every obstacle type in one phrase, one answer per half bar: jump, pad, jump, slide, gap, jump, jump, slide. Each landing sets up the next input.

patterns.name: Recovery
patterns.notes: Two jumps in four bars. Deliberately almost empty -- somewhere to put the player down after a climax so the next one lands.

patterns.name: Sustain
patterns.notes: Two long holds. Teaches press, keep holding, release.

patterns.name: Taps Into Hold
patterns.notes: A rising three-tap phrase that resolves into a sustain -- the shape of a sung line.

patterns.name: Drift Up
patterns.notes: One long note sliding lane 1 -> 4 over six beats. The first drift hold a player meets.

patterns.name: Drift Zigzag
patterns.notes: A drift that descends and comes back -- tracing a melody rather than a ramp.

patterns.name: Hold Plus Taps
patterns.notes: Left hand sustains while the right hand plays the accents.

patterns.name: Vertical Climax
patterns.notes: Chords, a run, then a descending drift with accents over the top.

patterns.name: Diagonal Cycle
patterns.notes: The four diagonals on their own, so two-key entry gets learned before it is mixed in.

patterns.name: Clockwise 8
patterns.notes: A full eight-step turn clockwise, one step per beat across two bars.

patterns.name: Counterclockwise 8
patterns.notes: The same turn reversed. Good A/B for whether the rotation direction reads.

patterns.name: Cardinal Diagonal Alternation
patterns.notes: Alternating one-key and two-key entries -- the hardest thing about eight directions.

patterns.name: Diagonal Opposite Pairs
patterns.notes: Both diagonal axes, one per half bar.

patterns.name: Spiral 8
patterns.notes: Cardinals first then diagonals, on eighths. Dense but the shape is a simple rule.

patterns.name: Star
patterns.notes: Skipping three steps each time draws a star. Feels unpredictable, is completely regular.

patterns.name: Radial Climax
patterns.notes: Four opposite pairs, then a full clockwise turn at double speed.

patterns.name: Platform Step
patterns.notes: Two low platforms: at 0.04 high the runner walks up without jumping, so the lesson is that a platform is terrain before it is an obstacle.

patterns.name: Platform Hop
patterns.notes: A single jump-height platform per bar. The front face is the obstacle and the top is the reward: land on it and the beat after is free.

patterns.name: Staircase Up
patterns.notes: Three risers on consecutive beats, each one higher than the last. Every step is a jump, and the landing of one is the take-off of the next.

patterns.name: Platform Ladder
patterns.notes: Platforms on the half-beat, alternating a low step and a full hop, with a spike on the ground at the end of the bar so the ground route is never the answer.

patterns.name: Gap Bridge
patterns.notes: A gap with a platform parked over its far side. The jump clears the gap, the platform is what the player lands on -- one obstacle doing two jobs.

patterns.name: Platform Leap
patterns.notes: A gap whose only landing is a high platform over the middle. The take-off is fixed by the gap edge, so the jump is committed to before the platform is under the player.

patterns.name: Gravity Shelf
patterns.notes: The flip arrives and the shelf is already on the ceiling: the player lands on the new surface a step above it, and the second shelf is a real jump.

patterns.name: Gravity Corridor
patterns.notes: Two flips, shelves on both surfaces, and a spike after the first flip so the ceiling is not optional. The read is which surface the next shelf belongs to.

patterns.name: Platform Climax
patterns.notes: The full vocabulary at once: a bridge, a ladder on the half-beat, a flip with a shelf already waiting, and a low wall closing the bar. No bar repeats the one before it.

patterns.name: Platform Recovery
patterns.notes: One low shelf per bar and nothing else: a landing beat the player can breathe on without the runner ever stopping.

patterns.name: Seal Break
patterns.notes: The teaching form: four cardinals, one per beat, resolving on the next downbeat. One bar of build-up, one bar of phrase, the accent on the bar line. Two misses are forgiven, so a first encounter is survivable while it is still being learned.

patterns.name: Seal Break Syncopated
patterns.notes: Six inputs mixing beats and half-beats, with a bar of anticipation before the accent on beat 5. The off-beats are what make it a phrase rather than a list, and the hexagonal seal gives the sharper rhythm a sharper silhouette.

patterns.name: Seal Break Gauntlet
patterns.notes: Eight inputs including a repeated direction and three half-beats, tighter windows, one forgiven miss and a heavier collapse. The hardest thing the mechanic can ask for that still leaves the seal escapable at every tempo.

patterns.name: Seal Break: First Step
patterns.notes: The first thing the mechanic ever asks for: two arrows, one per strong beat, then SPACE on the bar line. Nothing is timed except that last press, so a player who has never seen a seal can still find the rule inside one bar of reading. Three misses are forgiven, which at two inputs means the encounter cannot be failed at all -- that is deliberate for the first eight seconds of the song. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Three Ways
patterns.notes: Stage two of the teaching: three of the four cardinals, one per bar, so the phrase itself lasts two bars instead of one. The rhythm is deliberately left alone -- the player is being asked to hold three things in their head, not to read a harder rhythm. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Four Corners
patterns.notes: Stage three, and the first encounter a player can fail. The full clockwise circuit on four consecutive beats -- one input per beat is the densest thing in the teaching section, and it lands exactly where the drums enter. This is the shape the rest of the song is built from. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Double Tap
patterns.notes: Same length and same density as Four Corners with the directions arranged as pairs instead of a circuit. Two patterns back to back that differ only in how the arrows are grouped is the cheapest possible lesson in "the order matters, not the count". Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Crescendo
patterns.notes: A reprise of First Step, transformed on every axis the player can notice: two inputs became four, half notes became quarters, and the encounter moved from the bare vocal into the build. Same idea, played at the speed the music has now reached. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Arch
patterns.notes: The first half-beat in the level, arriving exactly where the drop does. It is a mirror: the offsets are symmetric about beat 3 and the directions read the same backwards, so the phrase is remembered as a shape rather than as five separate things. That is what makes a syncopated phrase fair this early. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Counter Circuit
patterns.notes: Four Corners walked the other way round. Identical rhythm and identical length to the teaching pattern, so the only new information is that counter-clockwise is a different answer from clockwise -- which is the thing a player who has been coasting on muscle memory needs to be told. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Stutter Step
patterns.notes: Six inputs in a four-beat phrase: three doubled cells with a beat of air in front of each. Still the repeat family, so nothing about the vocabulary is new -- only the rate. It is the first encounter in the level where the player has to move their hands rather than their memory. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Slow Sway
patterns.notes: Four inputs over two bars, on the vertical axis only. The breakdown is where the bass drops out, so the chart drops out too: half the density of the drop, a single axis, and a whole bar of silence before the accent. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Call and Answer
patterns.notes: Two inputs that ask a question on the horizontal axis and two that answer it on the vertical. The first time the level uses the phrase itself as the unit of meaning rather than the individual arrow. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Slow Arch
patterns.notes: Three inputs, two beats apart, symmetric about the middle one. The shortest phrase in the level and the slowest, sitting on the last bar of the breakdown so the player is completely idle when the build begins. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Long Circuit
patterns.notes: Six inputs, all on the beat, arriving as the build comes back under the breakdown. The circuit is the same one the teaching section taught; it is simply longer and no longer stops at four, which is the whole of the escalation here. The energy peak at bar 38 lands on the first input. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Long Echo
patterns.notes: A three-note call on beats 1-3 and its retrograde on beats 5-7, with beat 4 left empty as the hinge. Six inputs but only three things to remember, because the second half is the first half backwards -- the level teaching the player how to compress a phrase instead of asking them to hold more of it. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Long Arch
patterns.notes: Seven inputs, one per beat, symmetric in time and direction about beat 3. The longest phrase so far and the first that has to be held in memory as a whole; the symmetry is what keeps it inside working memory rather than turning it into a list. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Machine
patterns.notes: Six inputs on six consecutive half-beats, as three doubled cells. The peak of the second drop is the densest four beats in the level, and it is dense purely in rate: the vocabulary is still the repeat family, so the player is being asked to move faster, not to think harder. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Pendulum
patterns.notes: The second relief, on the axis the first relief did not use. Four inputs, one per beat, no memory load at all -- the point is that the hands keep moving while the music breathes, so the drop back in does not feel like a cold start. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Slow Circuit
patterns.notes: The circuit, clockwise from the bottom, at relief density. A reprise of Counter Circuit with the direction order rotated by one -- the same four answers in a different sequence, which is the cheapest way to keep a familiar shape from becoming a reflex. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Short Echo
patterns.notes: Five inputs: a three-note call and a two-note answer that is its retrograde. The last quiet encounter before the climax, and the only one in the second relief that asks for anything -- it is the ramp back up, arriving as the music starts to rise again at bar 61. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Surge
patterns.notes: Seven inputs: three doubled cells and then a single step into the accent. The rhythm is flat on purpose -- the surge is in the count, not the subdivision -- so that the last bar before the climax is a straight line rather than another thing to decode. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Full Circuit
patterns.notes: The teaching circuit twice over, eight inputs on eight beats. Nothing in it is new; it is the same four answers the level opened with, held for twice as long. The first encounter of the climax is deliberately the one the player already knows, so the section starts by rewarding them rather than testing them. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Grand Arch
patterns.notes: Nine inputs, symmetric in time about beat 3.5 and a palindrome in direction. The longest mirrored phrase in the level and the only one that puts a half-beat on every interior gap: the player reads the first half, and the second half is already decided. The one-bar energy drop at bar 68 lands on this encounter, so the seal is at its widest exactly when the music steps back. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Final Chain
patterns.notes: Ten inputs, and the only pattern in the level that chains four families into one phrase: an alternation, a three-step sweep, a doubled cell, and a four-note run into the accent. It is the last thing the song asks for and it resolves on the last downbeat of the track, with a heavier collapse behind it than anything else so that failing it is unambiguous. Two rounds: the phrase, then its mirror at double speed.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Swung Walk
patterns.notes: Drip Too Hard is a half-time record with a swung vocal, so the phrase is a triplet walk rather than an eighth-note one: five steps at two-thirds of a beat each, which is the subdivision the voice is actually using. Nothing lands on a strong beat except the accent, and that is the point -- the player is asked to feel the swing rather than count the grid. Two rounds, the phrase and its mirror, each resolving on a real downbeat four beats after it starts.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Call and Reply
patterns.notes: The call is four arrows, one per beat, filling a whole real bar. The reply is three arrows in half a bar -- the same idea answered in half the time. That long-then-short shape is the song's own call and response between the vocal and the drop, and it teaches a player to read phrase length as information instead of expecting a fixed number of inputs. Both accents land on downbeats.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Half-Time
patterns.notes: A doubled cell, a beat and a half of nothing, then a second doubled cell running into the accent. The hole is authored rather than accidental: a player who reads ahead sees the gap and has to hold position through it instead of filling it. On a half-time record the silence is the loudest part of the bar, so the phrase spends its steps exactly where the track does and rests where the track rests.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Offbeat
patterns.notes: Six arrows in three beats with the second one missing: the cell doubles on the first half-beat and then skips the beat it would have landed on. The skip is what makes it read as syncopation rather than as a run -- the hand wants to press on that beat and has to not. One miss forgiven, because the first time a player meets a hole in a stream they will press into it.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Pressure
patterns.notes: Seven arrows, one per half-beat, straight through the bar and into the accent. This is the plainest thing the mechanic can ask for at this tempo and it is here on purpose: after the swing and the syncopation of the first drop, the loudest bars of the record ask for an even stream a player can lock onto. The pressure is the tempo, not the shape, which is why one miss is forgiven and the collapse behind it is heavy.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Triplet Storm
patterns.notes: The swung walk again, but where it used to end it now doubles: four triplet steps, then three in the last beat. A player who learned the walk in the first drop recognises the opening and then has to accelerate inside a subdivision they thought they knew. That recognition-then-subversion is what makes a climax read as a climax rather than as a longer version of the same thing.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Finale
patterns.notes: Three rounds in one pattern, and the only dance pattern in the library that asks for a third: an even six, a swung six, then a short three that resolves on the last beat of the pattern. The rounds are the same length on paper and different lengths in the hand, so the phrase cannot be memorised as a list -- it has to be read. It closes the level on the bar the record closes on, and the collapse behind it is heavy so that failing the last thing the song asks for is unambiguous.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Pulse
patterns.notes: Four arrows inside a beat and a fifth, then the accent on the very next bar line. At 129 BPM that is a press every 190ms, fast enough that the phrase has to be read as a shape rather than as four separate decisions, and the reward is an accent landing on the downbeat of the loudest track in the library. The mirror starts two beats later, so both accents land on bar lines and the pattern reads as a pulse rather than as a run.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Push
patterns.notes: Five eighth-note steps and then three full beats of nothing before the accent lands on beat four. The gap is the mechanic: the player finishes the phrase early and has to hold the beat they were given instead of pressing when their hands are ready. Beat four is where this track pushes into the next bar, so the accent is authored to arrive with the push rather than with the downbeat it pushes toward.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Stomp
patterns.notes: The same direction twice, three times over, then the accent on beat four. Doubled cells are how a four-on-the-floor record asks for weight rather than speed -- the hand comes back to the key it just left instead of travelling, which is a different motion from a run even at the same tempo. The accent on beat four keeps the push feel this family uses for the track, so the phrase ends leaning into the next bar.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Roll
patterns.notes: Seven arrows across three beats, resolving on the downbeat of the bar after next, then a three-arrow reply that resolves on the downbeat after that. The long round is long enough to leave working memory and has to be read as a continuous roll; the short round is the same idea compressed, so the two accents arrive two beats apart with nothing between them. It is the only pattern in the family whose rounds differ in length and share a resolution point.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Break
patterns.notes: Seven arrows with one missing, and the missing one is the beat the player has been taught to press on. The hole sits where this family usually puts a step, so a player running on muscle memory will press into it and lose the phrase -- reading the row is the only way through. It is the hardest reading demand in the library at this tempo, which is why the accent lands on beat four rather than on a downbeat: the reward is the push, not the resolution.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Torrent
patterns.notes: Eight arrows, one per half-beat: four beats of continuous input and then the accent on beat four of the next bar. There is no trick in the shape and that is deliberate -- at 129 BPM a plain eight is already at the edge of what a hand can do without a break, and the pattern exists to find out whether a player can keep an even stream going when nothing in the phrase tells them where they are. One miss forgiven, heavy collapse behind it.

patterns.name: Seal Break: Last Stand
patterns.notes: Four rounds and thirty-one inputs: an even eight, then two nines that end in a sixteenth cluster, then a short five that closes on beat four of the last bar. Each round is a little longer than the last and every accent still lands where this family puts it for the track, so the phrase escalates in load without ever moving its resolution. It is the last thing the level asks for and it ends on the last musical bar of the record.
